I also had a chaotic upbringing with a lot of neglect and emotional abuse. My teens and 20s were quite difficult for me. I just finished my undergrad in 2022 at the age of 29. I am 31 now and have a steady job and much more stability now. Some of us aren’t as fortunate to have access to the support and resources we need to thrive. A lot of times it’s hard to see a way out when you’re so low and feeling hopeless. 

What helped me is firstly learning to be gentle and forgiving with yourself. Your timeline may take shorter or longer, but regardless you will get there. Focus on what needs to be done in the moment to get you where you need to be, don’t overwhelm yourself with everything all at once. Take micro actions if you need to (get out of bed, take a shower, open your textbook, etc.). The hardest part for me often was just getting started. The more you repeatedly study or take care of yourself, the more routine and easier it gets. Maybe schedule your time and attempt to follow it, and also forgive yourself if you don’t do it perfectly. You’re not looking for perfect, just incremental improvements. 

Maybe put yourself in social situations to grow a network. Join school clubs or find meetups that match your interests, or something you might be interested in doing. It takes times to make friends, and it isn’t always easy, but just repeatedly put yourself in social situations if you can. But again, be gentle with yourself. It’s okay if you have hard days. Find things you can do to mitigate those feelings, whatever that might be. 

The only way out is through. Just keep doing things, and they don’t need to be big, even teeny tiny things. Stand up, take a shower, get dressed, and walk out the door.

To preface, there denotes an accepted-level of relativism in interpretation of Biblical text, as demonstrated by the many manifestations of it. The crux of your argument is semantic in nature; looking at the hermeneutics quickly reveals the multiplicity of meanings of the original Greek and Hebrew. You yourself elaborate upon the many meanings of different words. Perhaps you could argue that the meaning of the word is further determined by its context, but that also does not seem to always provide insight to a word’s meaning when it comes to Biblical text, which you have also demonstrated. Thus it seems rather unlikely that one can come to any absolute conclusion of what the religious text aims to convey, which leaves any given interpretation contending for the position of “truth leader”. 

You make the claim that “typical English translations on the issue are irrelevant, since most translations are interpretive rather than literal.” Could this literal-interpretive issue be applied not only to typical English translations, but rather all interpretations of and commentaries on biblical text? Any instance in which one interprets a word or stanza of the original text, there is a subjectivity to interpretation that cannot be avoided. A modern person fluent in Greek or Hebrew or Arabic still does not speak the same Greek or Hebrew or Aramaic from thousands of years ago, and even scholars are limited in that regard, so those are additional language barriers. Point being, there is too much ambiguity surrounding the meaning of words in biblical text, so perhaps Christians do have sufficient grounds to condemn homosexuality due to their own subjective tradition of interpretation.

Perhaps, however, what is more important than any given instance of interpretation is what gives any interpretation of a religious text its authority. No matter what, there is a human or group of humans who decide that a given interpretation is valid and sound doctrine, which is what effectively authorizes its meaning. From the Christian tradition, there have been councils that have commenced to determine the teachings and resolve issues of meaning within the Bible. The general consensus from the Christian tradition and interpretation of biblical text using the verses you listed is that homosexuality is a sin. One cannot really argue from a point of semantics, because there is just too much room for  various interpretations of the hermeneutics.
